title: Getting Started: Overview of spacemodR
text: Everything starts geography. spacemodR facilitates extraction manipulation land cover data (like OCS-GE database France) given Region Interest (ROI). First, load data site northern France. , use provided data (ocsge_metaleurop roi_metaleurop) along ggplot2 package visualization.  vector polygons, define habitats species. habitat combination favorable, unfavorable, neutral zones. geometries rasterized (converted regular grids) prepare modeling.  habitat specificities included project. Currently, 935 species, including 499 birds, 215 mammals, 136 reptiles, 85 amphibians. example, common vole (Microtus arvalis):  … greater white-toothed shrew (Crocidura russula):  understand 3 maps detail, please refer Habitat page. Briefly: Suitability: carrying capacity (general attractiveness) environment species. Foraging weight: trophic attractiveness environment. animal necessarily feed everywhere lives. Resistance (Movement resistance / Spatial friction): energetic cost danger associated crossing environment, 1 (free movement) 100 (impassable). parameter used connectivity dispersal models (like Omniscape algorithm discussed later). stage, now habitats defined, rasterize habitats based default layer, cd_ground. allows us landscape grid can successfully overlay layers.
code: # Load a study area (e.g., the Metaleurop site) and its land cover data data("roi_metaleurop") data("ocsge_metaleurop")  ggplot() +   theme_minimal() +   geom_sf(data=ocsge_metaleurop, aes(fill=code_cs), color=NA) +   geom_sf(data=roi_metaleurop, fill=NA, color="red", size=1) +   theme(legend.position = "none") +   labs(title="Land Cover in the Region of Interest (ROI)") # Example: Loading a background concentration raster for a contaminant (Cadmium) ground_cd <- load_raster_extdata("ground_concentration_cd_compressed.tif")  # Habitat definition based on OSGE codes (which are in the `ocsge_metaleurop` table) layer_soil_natural = ocsge_metaleurop$code_cs %in%    c("CS1.2.1","CS2.1.1.1","CS2.1.1.2","CS2.1.1.3", "CS2.1.2","CS2.1.3","CS2.2.1","CS2.2.3") layer_soil_artificial = ocsge_metaleurop$code_cs %in%   c("CS1.1.1.1", "CS1.1.1.2", "CS1.1.2.1") layer_plant = ocsge_metaleurop$code_cs %in%     c("CS2.1.1.1", "CS2.1.1.2", "CS2.1.1.3", "CS2.1.3", "CS2.2.1") habitat_sol = habitat() |>   add_habitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_soil_natural,]) |>   add_nohabitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_soil_artificial,]) plot(habitat_sol) habitat_plante = habitat() |>   add_habitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_plant,]) |>   add_nohabitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_soil_artificial,]) microtus_hab <- join_ocsge_species(ocsge_metaleurop, "Microtus_arvalis") plot_species_habitat(microtus_hab) crocidura_hab <- join_ocsge_species(ocsge_metaleurop, "Crocidura") plot_species_habitat(crocidura_hab) # We use `suitability` as habitat weight, and take out the covers the species cannot cross habitat_herbivore <- habitat(microtus_hab, habitat=TRUE, weight=microtus_hab$suitability) |>   add_nohabitat(microtus_hab[microtus_hab$permeability==0,]) habitat_carnivore <- habitat(crocidura_hab, habitat=TRUE, weight=crocidura_hab$suitability) |>   add_nohabitat(crocidura_hab[crocidura_hab$permeability==0,]) # We initialize habitat grids (rasters) for each level rast_sol <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_sol) rast_plant <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_plante) rast_herbivor <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_herbivore) rast_carnivor <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_carnivore)  # We create the `raster_stack` of the habitats stack_habitat <- raster_stack(   raster_list = list(rast_sol, rast_plant, rast_herbivor, rast_carnivor),   names = c("soil", "plant", "herbivore", "carnivore") )  terra::plot(stack_habitat)

title: Getting Started: Overview of spacemodR
text: Animals static. individual’s exposure depends movements (foraging radius, dispersal). spacemodR allows simulate movements, instance via convolution kernels circuit theory (Omniscape).
code: # Compute dispersal kernels based on a mobility radius (e.g., in pixels) k_herb <- compute_kernel(radius=50, GSD=25, size_std=0.5) k_carn <- compute_kernel(radius=150, GSD=25, size_std=0.5)  # Apply dispersal to the spacemodel spcmdl_dispersal <- spcmdl |>   dispersal("herbivore", method="convolution", method_option=list(kernel=k_herb)) |>   dispersal("carnivore", method="convolution", method_option=list(kernel=k_carn))  # Note: In this example, the soil and plants are static and do not disperse.

title: Getting Started: Overview of spacemodR
text: Now system set , can “inject” actual pollutant concentrations soil, model bioconcentration bioaccumulation top food chain using transfer() function.
code: # 1. Assign the actual concentration grid into the "soil" layer spcmdl_dispersal[["soil"]][] <- terra::values(ground_cd)  # 2. Define the transfer equations (Bioaccumulation / Bioconcentration Factors) fluxes <- flux(spcmdl_dispersal, default = 1) |>   add_flux("soil", "plant",  ~ 10^x / 32) |> # Specific equation for plants   add_flux("soil", "herbivore",  0.5) |>     # Simple transfer factor for the herbivore   add_flux("herbivore", "carnivore",  0.8)   # Simple transfer factor for the carnivore  # 3. Gather our dispersal kernels for the exposure calculation kernels <- list(soil = NA, plant = NA, herbivore = k_herb, carnivore = k_carn)  # 4. Compute the global transfer throughout the ecosystem spcmdl_transfer <- transfer(spcmdl_dispersal, kernels, fluxes)  # Visualize the contamination absorbed by the carnivore color_transfer <- colorRampPalette(c("white", "#A33D0A"))(255) terra::plot(spcmdl_transfer, col=color_transfer)

title: Getting Started: Overview of spacemodR
text: final step ERA often involves generating Risk Index (e.g., Hazard Quotient Eco-SSL approach). allows us map “Hot-Spots” ecotoxicological reference thresholds exceeded.
code: # Define risk classes (from "Safe" to "Very High Risk") breaks_risk <- c(-Inf, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, Inf) cols_risk <- c(   "darkgreen",   # 0 - 0.1 (No Risk)   "green",       # 0.1 - 0.5   "lightgreen",  # 0.5 - 1 (Threshold limit)   "yellow",      # 1 - 5 (Moderate Risk)   "saddlebrown", # 5 - 10 (High Risk)   "#4A2C2A"      # > 10 (Severe Risk) )  # Project the risk onto the Region of Interest poly_vect <- terra::project(terra::vect(roi_metaleurop), terra::crs(spcmdl_transfer)) rast_crop <- terra::crop(spcmdl_transfer[["herbivore"]], poly_vect) rast_final <- terra::mask(rast_crop, poly_vect)  terra::plot(rast_final,             breaks = breaks_risk,             col = cols_risk,             main = "Risk Index Map (Herbivore)")

title: Getting Started: Vue d'ensemble de spacemodR
text: Tout commence par la géographie. spacemodR facilite l’extraction et la manipulation de données d’occupation du sol (comme la base OCS-GE en France) pour une zone d’intérêt (Region Interest - ROI). Nous chargeons dans un premier temps les données d’un site dans le nord de la France. Ici, utilise les présente (ocsge_metaleurop et roi_metaleurop) ainsi que le package ggplot2 pour la représentation.  À partir de ces polygones, nous définissons des habitats pour nos espèces. Un habitat est une combinaison de zones favorables, défavorables ou neutres. Ces géométries sont ensuite transformées en grilles régulières (rasters) prêtes pour la modélisation.  Certaines de ces spécificités d’habitats sont incluses dans le projet. Pour l’instant, 935 espèces dont 499 oiseaux, 215 mammifères, 136 reptiles et 85 amphibiens. Par exemple pour le campagnol des champs (Microtus arvalis):  … et la musaraigne grise commune (Crocidura russula):  Pour comprendre les 3 cartes en détails, ce référer à la page Habitat. Brièvement: Suitability (qualité d’habitat), c’est la capacité d’accueil (ou l’attractivité générale) d’un milieu pour l’espèce. Foraging weight (pondération de recherche de nourriture) : c’est l’attractivité trophique du milieu. Un animal ne se nourrit pas forcément partout où il vit. Resistance (résistance au déplacement / Friction spatiale) : c’est le coût énergétique ou le danger lié à la traversée de ce milieu, de 1 (déplacement libre) à 100 (infranchissable). Ce paramètre est utilisé par les modèles de connectivité et de dispersion (comme l’algorithme Omniscape abordé plus tard). cette étape, maintenant que les habitats sont défini, rasterize les habitats selon une couche par défaut, ici cd_ground, qui va permettre d’avoir la même grille paysagère afin de pouvoir superposer toutes les couches.
code: # Charger une zone d'étude (ex: site de Metaleurop) et les données d'occupation du sol data("roi_metaleurop") data("ocsge_metaleurop")  ggplot() +   theme_minimal() +   geom_sf(data=ocsge_metaleurop, aes(fill=code_cs), color=NA) +   geom_sf(data=roi_metaleurop, fill=NA, color="red", size=1) +   theme(legend.position = "none") +   labs(title="Occupation du sol sur la zone d'étude") # Exemple: Chargement d'un raster de la concentration de fond d'un contaminant (Cadmium) ground_cd <- load_raster_extdata("ground_concentration_cd_compressed.tif")  # Définition d'habitat à partir des code OSGE (qui sont dans le tableau `ocsge_metaleurop`) layer_soil_natural = ocsge_metaleurop$code_cs %in%    c("CS1.2.1","CS2.1.1.1","CS2.1.1.2","CS2.1.1.3", "CS2.1.2","CS2.1.3","CS2.2.1","CS2.2.3") layer_soil_artificial = ocsge_metaleurop$code_cs %in%   c("CS1.1.1.1", "CS1.1.1.2", "CS1.1.2.1") layer_plant = ocsge_metaleurop$code_cs %in%     c("CS2.1.1.1", "CS2.1.1.2", "CS2.1.1.3", "CS2.1.3", "CS2.2.1") habitat_sol = habitat() |>   add_habitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_soil_natural,]) |>   add_nohabitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_soil_artificial,]) plot(habitat_sol) habitat_plante = habitat() |>   add_habitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_plant,]) |>   add_nohabitat(ocsge_metaleurop[layer_soil_artificial,]) microtus_hab <- join_ocsge_species(ocsge_metaleurop, "Microtus_arvalis") plot_species_habitat(microtus_hab) crocidura_hab <- join_ocsge_species(ocsge_metaleurop, "Crocidura") plot_species_habitat(crocidura_hab) # nous utilisons `suitability` comme poids d'habitat, et retirons les couvertures infranchissables pour l'espèce habitat_herbivore <- habitat(microtus_hab, habitat=TRUE, weight=microtus_hab$suitability) |>   add_nohabitat(microtus_hab[microtus_hab$permeability==0,]) habitat_carnivore <- habitat(crocidura_hab, habitat=TRUE, weight=crocidura_hab$suitability) |>   add_nohabitat(crocidura_hab[crocidura_hab$permeability==0,]) # On initialise des grilles d'habitats (raster) pour chaque maillon rast_sol <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_sol) rast_plant <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_plante) rast_herbivor <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_herbivore) rast_carnivor <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, habitat_carnivore)  # On créé le `raster_stack` des habiats stack_habitat <- raster_stack(   raster_list = list(rast_sol, rast_plant, rast_herbivor, rast_carnivor),   names = c("sol", "plante", "herbivore", "carnivore") )  terra::plot(stack_habitat)

title: Getting Started: Vue d'ensemble de spacemodR
text: Une fois nos cartes créées, nous devons relier ces couches par des interactions écologiques. spacemodR utilise un Graphe Orienté Acyclique (DAG) pour définir les proies, les prédateurs, et le flux de l’énergie (ou des contaminants).
code: # Construction du réseau trophique trophic_df <- trophic() |>   add_link(from = "sol", to = "plante") |>   add_link(from = "plante", to = "herbivore") |>   add_link(from = "herbivore", to = "carnivore")  # Visualisation des liens trophiques plot(trophic_df)

title: Getting Started: Vue d'ensemble de spacemodR
text: Le spacemodel est le cœur du package. Il lie intrinsèquement la dimension spatiale (le raster_stack) et la dimension écologique (le graphe trophic_df). Toute opération ultérieure (dispersion, exposition) utilisera cet objet pour garantir la cohérence des calculs.
code: spcmdl <- spacemodel(stack_habitat, trophic_df) print(spcmdl) #> class       : SpatRaster #> size        : 415, 401, 4  (nrow, ncol, nlyr) #> resolution  : 24.93766, 24.93976  (x, y) #> extent      : 697602.7, 707602.7, 7032171, 7042521  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) #> coord. ref. : RGF93 v1 / Lambert-93 (EPSG:2154) #> source(s)   : memory #> varnames    : ground_concentration_cd_compressed #>               ground_concentration_cd_compressed #>               ground_concentration_cd_compressed #>               ground_concentration_cd_compressed #> names       : sol, plante, herbivore, carnivore #> min values  :   0,      0,         0,         0 #> max values  :   1,      1,        10,         8

title: Getting Started: Vue d'ensemble de spacemodR
text: Les animaux ne sont pas statiques. L’exposition d’un individu dépend de ses déplacements (son rayon de recherche de nourriture, sa dispersion). spacemodR permet de simuler ces mouvements, par exemple via des noyaux de convolution (kernels) ou la théorie des circuits (Omniscape).
code: # Calcul des noyaux de dispersion en fonction d'un rayon de mobilité (ex: en pixels) k_herb <- compute_kernel(radius=50, GSD=25, size_std=0.5) k_carn <- compute_kernel(radius=150, GSD=25, size_std=0.5)  # Application de la dispersion sur le spacemodel spcmdl_dispersal <- spcmdl |>   dispersal("herbivore", method="convolution", method_option=list(kernel=k_herb)) |>   dispersal("carnivore", method="convolution", method_option=list(kernel=k_carn))  # Note : le sol et les plantes sont évidemment statiques et ne dispersent pas.

title: Getting Started: Vue d'ensemble de spacemodR
text: Maintenant que le système est en place, nous pouvons “injecter” la concentration de notre polluant dans le sol, et modéliser sa bioconcentration et sa bioaccumulation jusqu’au sommet de la chaîne alimentaire grâce à la fonction transfer().
code: # 1. On assigne la grille de concentration réelle dans la couche "soil" spcmdl_dispersal[["sol"]][] <- terra::values(ground_cd)  # 2. On définit les équations de transfert (Facteurs de Bioaccumulation / Bioconcentration) fluxes <- flux(spcmdl_dispersal, default = 1) |>   add_flux("soil", "plant",  ~ 10^x / 32) |> # Equation spécifique pour les plantes   add_flux("soil", "herbivore",  0.5) |>     # Facteur simple pour l'herbivore   add_flux("herbivore", "carnivore",  0.8)   # Facteur simple pour le carnivore  # 3. On rassemble nos noyaux de dispersion pour le calcul de l'exposition kernels <- list(sol = NA, plante = NA, herbivore = k_herb, carnivore = k_carn)  # 4. Calcul du transfert global dans l'écosystème spcmdl_transfer <- transfer(spcmdl_dispersal, kernels, fluxes)  # Visualisation de la contamination absorbée par le carnivore color_transfer <- colorRampPalette(c("white", "#A33D0A"))(255) terra::plot(spcmdl_transfer, col=color_transfer)

title: Getting Started: Vue d'ensemble de spacemodR
text: L’étape finale de l’ERA consiste souvent à générer un Indice de Risque (par exemple, le Quotient de Danger ou l’approche Eco-SSL). Cela permet de cartographier les “Hot-Spots” où les seuils de toxicité de référence sont dépassés.
code: # Définition des classes de risque (de "Sûr" à "Risque Très Élevé") breaks_risk <- c(-Inf, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, Inf) cols_risk <- c(   "darkgreen",   # 0 - 0.1 (Pas de risque)   "green",       # 0.1 - 0.5   "lightgreen",  # 0.5 - 1 (Limite)   "yellow",      # 1 - 5 (Risque modéré)   "saddlebrown", # 5 - 10 (Risque fort)   "#4A2C2A"      # > 10 (Risque très sévère) )  # Projection du risque sur la zone d'étude poly_vect <- terra::project(terra::vect(roi_metaleurop), terra::crs(spcmdl_transfer)) rast_crop <- terra::crop(spcmdl_transfer[["herbivore"]], poly_vect) rast_final <- terra::mask(rast_crop, poly_vect)  terra::plot(rast_final,             breaks = breaks_risk,             col = cols_risk,             main = "Cartographie de l'Indice de Risque (Herbivore)")

title: Getting Started: Vue d'ensemble de spacemodR
text: Vous venez de voir l’ensemble du pipeline spacemodR en action ! Pour aller plus loin et configurer finement chaque étape, nous vous invitons à consulter nos guides spécialisés : 🧩️ Habitat Layer : Construire des cartes de résistance et d’habitats complexes depuis des vecteurs. 🧩️ Landscape Connectivity : Intégrer la théorie des circuits (Omniscape) pour le mouvement des grands mammifères. 🎯️ Tuning Parameters: Faire l’inférence des paramètres (méthodes Bayesiennes). 🧪 Example Zoo : Explorer des cas d’études réels (comme le modèle Berisp complet).

title: Food Intake Rate
text: Assignation de la Densité Énergétique (kJ/gkJ/g MS) : Végétaux : Utiliser les valeurs LCV de la base TRY. Invertébrés : Appliquer le modèle AFDW (log10(ED)=1,07×log10(AFDW)−0,80log_{10}(ED) = 1,07 \times log_{10}(AFDW) - 0,80) ou les constantes de Cummins & Wuycheck. Vertébrés : Utiliser le paramètre ξWE\xi_{} de Add--pet. Une avancée significative dans l’estimation de la densité énergétique repose sur l’utilisation du pourcentage d’AFDW. Le poids sec total (DWDW) inclut souvent des composants inorganiques non digestibles comme les os, les coquilles ou les sels, qui varient considérablement entre les organismes et peuvent fausser les estimations énergétiques. En isolant la fraction organique, le modèle AFDW permet d’estimer la densité énergétique des invertébrés, des vertébrés et des plantes avec une seule équation.L’équation de régression globale identifiée est :log⁡10(ED)=1,07×log⁡10(AFDW)−0,80\log_{10}(ED) = 1,07 \times \log_{10}(AFDW) - 0,80

title: Habitat Data Sources
text: map raster, join reclassification. write small helper replaces EUNIS class species score. combined codes "D5/F6", scores two classes averaged.
code: eunis_species_raster <- function(lc, species, var = "suitability",                                  dict = eunis_species_dict) {   lv <- terra::levels(lc)[[1]]   names(lv) <- c("value", "code")   d <- dict[dict$species_name == species, ]   if (nrow(d) == 0) stop("Species not found: ", species)   val <- vapply(strsplit(lv$code, "/"),                 function(cc) mean(d[[var]][match(cc, d$code_eunis)]), numeric(1))   r <- lc   levels(r) <- NULL                       # drop categories, keep pixel ids   out <- terra::classify(r, cbind(lv$value, val))   names(out) <- var   out } vars <- c("suitability", "weight_breeding", "weight_foraging", "resistance") microtus_eunis <- rast(lapply(vars, function(v) eunis_species_raster(eunis_lc, "Microtus_arvalis", v)))  p_score <- ggplot() +   geom_spatraster(data = microtus_eunis[[1:3]]) +   facet_wrap(~lyr) +   scale_fill_gradient(low = "#ffffe5", high = "#004529", limits = c(0, 10),                       na.value = "transparent", name = "Score") +   theme_void() p_res <- ggplot() +   geom_spatraster(data = microtus_eunis[["resistance"]]) +   scale_fill_gradient(low = "#fff5f0", high = "#67000d", trans = "log10", limits = c(1, 100),                       na.value = "transparent", name = "Resistance") +   theme_void() +   labs(title = "resistance (1–100, log scale)")  p_score / p_res + plot_annotation(title = "Microtus arvalis – habitat layers from EUNIS")

title: Using Julia Omniscape to run Landscape Connectivity
text: Standard connectivity models usually ask: “get Point Point B?” Omniscape asks: “individuals start everywhere try move directions within home range, go? paths get used ?” applies Circuit Theory: treats landscape like electrical circuit board. Individuals = Electrons (Current). Landscape difficulty = Resistance.

what: The Inputs (What you give the model)
title: Using Julia Omniscape to run Landscape Connectivity
text: run Omniscape, primarily need two raster maps one parameter. Source Strength (Input Raster): Population Density map (number individuals/pixel). tells algorithm much current (amperes) inject pixel. Example: pixel value 100 (100 individuals), algorithm starts large “flow” movement spot. pixel value 0 (empty ground), movement starts (movement can still pass ). Resistance Surface (Input Raster): difficulty moving pixel. Arbitrary resistance unit (Ohms), usually 1 100. Example: Low value (1): Easy cross (e.g., preferred habitat), “current” flows easily . High value (100): Hard cross (e.g., wall, water, road), “current” blocked tries find way around. Infinite (NA): absolute barrier, flow possible. Radius (Parameter): dispersal distance home range (pixels). maximum distance individual likely travel. algorithm solves connectivity problem within moving window.

what: About Units of Source, Resistance and Radius
title: Using Julia Omniscape to run Landscape Connectivity
text: Source: relative capacity suitability (usually suitability weight_foraging internal ocsge_species_dict dataset). instance: Value 10 (Core habitat): dense, undisturbed forest fox. generates massive amount dispersing individuals. Value 2 (Poor habitat): small, degraded woodlot. emits individuals. Value 0 NA (Non-habitat): parking lot. emits absolutely individuals (though might still walk across resistance allows ). Resistance: Relative friction cost. absolute minimum 1 (perfect, frictionless movement). can never 0 negative. Effectively exponential/logarithmic. instance: Value 1 (Optimal): continuous forest. animal moves freely. Value 10 (Sub-optimal): tall grassland. animal can cross , takes energy, prefer forest ’s nearby. Value 100 (Hostile): plowed agricultural field. animal actively avoid cross absolutely choice reach next habitat. Value 1000 10000 (Absolute Barrier): fenced highway urban center. cost high model force animal take massive detour (e.g., walking 50 pixels way 1 resistance rather crossing single pixel 1000).

what: Step 2 — The large-scale trend: distance to the smelter
title: Soil contamination maps by kriging
text: Contamination comes atmospheric fallout single point source: smelter chimney. data set gives distance sample smelter (dist), smelter location . recover looking point whose distance every sample best matches dist (simple least-squares triangulation): match almost perfect (1 m), point lies 3.0162° E, 50.4287° N, .e. former Metaleurop site Noyelles-Godault.  Plotting concentrations distance log-log scale reveals strong linear trend: concentrations decrease power law distance, expected atmospheric deposition.  distance alone explains half variance log10(Cd). precious information interpolation, especially far samples: ordinary kriging predict global mean data, whereas model including distance keeps decreasing away smelter. motivates testing kriging external drift .
code: xy <- sf::st_coordinates(soil_metaleurop) misfit <- function(p) {   sum((sqrt((xy[, 1] - p[1])^2 + (xy[, 2] - p[2])^2) - soil_metaleurop$dist)^2) } fit <- optim(colMeans(xy), misfit) smelter <- sf::st_sfc(sf::st_point(fit$par), crs = 2154) smelter #> Geometry set for 1 feature  #> Geometry type: POINT #> Dimension:     XY #> Bounding box:  xmin: 701155.8 ymin: 7036798 xmax: 701155.8 ymax: 7036798 #> Projected CRS: RGF93 v1 / Lambert-93 # average mismatch with the `dist` column (m): sqrt(fit$value / nrow(xy)) #> [1] 1.035147 ggplot() +   geom_sf(data = soil_metaleurop, aes(colour = log10(cd)), size = 1.8) +   geom_sf(data = smelter, shape = 8, size = 5, colour = "red", stroke = 1.5) +   scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "log10 Cd\n(mg/kg)") +   labs(title = "Sampling points (red star: smelter)") +   theme_minimal() long$dist <- rep(soil_metaleurop$dist, 3) ggplot(long, aes(log10(dist), log10(value))) +   geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +   geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "red") +   facet_wrap(~metal, scales = "free_y") +   labs(x = "log10(distance to smelter, m)", y = "log10(concentration)") +   theme_minimal() summary(lm(log10(cd) ~ log10(dist), data = soil_metaleurop))$r.squared #> [1] 0.5028893

title: Soil contamination maps by kriging
text: Kriging relies one idea: two close samples alike two distant samples. semi-variogram quantifies : pairs points separated distance hh (grouped distance classes, lags), γ(h)=12N(h)∑(,j):dij≈h(zi−zj)2\gamma(h) = \frac{1}{2 N(h)} \sum_{(,j) \,:\, d_{ij} \approx h} \left(z_i - z_j\right)^2 zz log10 concentration N(h)N(h) number pairs. variogram increases hh means spatial structure kriging can exploit. soil_variogram() computes . default uses distances one third study area diagonal (cutoff) 15 classes (width). drift used (KED), spatial structure must described residuals trend, raw values; done passing covariates:  Reading plot: raw variogram keeps increasing several kilometres: signature large-scale trend (values decrease distance smelter); trend removed, residual variogram half high almost flat beyond 1–1.5 km: remaining spatial dependence short-range, long-range part explained distance; neither curve starts 0: value origin nugget, .e. variability close samples (measurement error, local heterogeneity, extreme outlier data set…).
code: v_ok <- soil_variogram(soil_metaleurop, "cd") head(v_ok) #>     np      dist      gamma #> 1 1260  174.5234 0.05594691 #> 2 3429  396.6164 0.06124015 #> 3 5228  648.8699 0.08059952 #> 4 6849  904.2774 0.09498779 #> 5 8100 1159.0879 0.12406657 #> 6 9379 1415.9839 0.13137464 v_ked <- soil_variogram(soil_metaleurop, "cd",                         covariates = covariates[["log10_dist"]]) both <- rbind(   data.frame(as.data.frame(unclass(v_ok)), type = "raw values (OK)"),   data.frame(as.data.frame(unclass(v_ked)), type = "residuals of log10(dist) (KED)") ) ggplot(both, aes(dist, gamma, colour = type)) +   geom_point(aes(size = np)) + geom_line() +   expand_limits(y = 0) +   labs(x = "Distance h (m)", y = expression(gamma(h)),        colour = NULL, size = "Number of pairs",        title = "Empirical variograms of log10(Cd)") +   theme_minimal()

title: Soil contamination maps by kriging
text: Kriging needs continuous function γ(h)\gamma(h), model fitted empirical points. Every model three parameters: nugget c0c_0: jump origin; partial sill cc: additional variance reached large distances (total sill = nugget + partial sill); range aa: fast sill reached (distance samples stop correlated 3a3a exponential model, aa spherical one). text: k-fold cross-validation (cv_soil()), points split 10 groups. group removed turn, whole method (including variogram fit) run 9 groups, removed points predicted. Comparing predictions observations gives: RMSE (root mean squared error, log10 units) — main criterion, lower better; MAE (mean absolute error) — less sensitive outlier; bias (mean error) — close 0; R2 — share variance data reproduced predictions. Two ways making groups used: random folds: removed points usually close neighbours left, measures quality interpolation samples; spatial folds (block_size = 1500): whole 1.5 km × 1.5 km blocks removed, mimics prediction areas without sample nearby (e.g. margin map). block size order distance residual variogram flattens.

title: Calibration of Transfer Models
text: likelihood defined : yi∼𝒩(μi,σ2) y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma^2) μi=β0+β1xi+βcat[x_cati] \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \beta_{\text{cat}}[x\_cat_i]  : β0\beta_0 global intercept. β1\beta_1 slope coefficient continuous variable xx. βcat[x_cati]\beta_{\text{cat}}[x\_cat_i] specific coefficient (effect) associated category observation ii belongs. σ\sigma standard deviation error term (residuals). model specifies weakly informative priors parameters regularize inferences without overly constraining data: Intercept: β0∼𝒩(0,10)\beta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10) Continuous Slope: β1∼𝒩(0,10)\beta_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10) Categorical Coefficients: βcat∼𝒩(0,10)\beta_{\text{cat}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10) KK categories. Error Standard Deviation: σ∼Half-Cauchy(0,5)\sigma \sim \text{Half-Cauchy}(0, 5). σ\sigma constrained strictly positive (real<lower=0> sigma;) , Cauchy prior automatically becomes truncated Half-Cauchy distribution. Based structure likelihood function, model makes following classical linear regression assumptions: Linearity: relationship continuous predictor xx mean response yy strictly linear. Additivity (Interactions): effect continuous variable (xx) categorical variable (xcatx_{cat}) purely additive. slopes assumed identical across categories; intercepts vary (parallel lines model). Normality Errors: residuals (differences observed predicted values) normally distributed. Homoscedasticity (Constant Variance): standard deviation error term, σ\sigma, assumed constant across values xx across KK categories. Independence: observation ii conditionally independent given parameters.

text: several pathways contamination, can divided two main categories: Direct contamination: occurs organism absorbs pollutant directly environment. Examples include fish exposed waterborne contaminants, earthworm absorbing pollutants soil, flying arthropods birds exposed airborne pollutants. single organism can also multiple direct exposure routes; instance, benthic (sediment-dwelling) invertebrates can contaminated sediment overlying water. model , simple equation usually sufficient, potentially accounting environmental properties (e.g., soil pH, organic matter, clay percentage) species-specific traits (e.g., plant might modify soil-plant interaction). Trophic contamination: refers contamination dietary intake. accurately model route, necessary know organism’s diet composition (food items consumed), biomass flux per kilogram individual, contaminant flux, calculated estimating contaminant concentration within specific food resource. second challenging aspect model differentiating exposures (doses organisms exposed) accumulated concentrations. organisms undergoing direct exposure, need calculate dietary contamination fluxes. organism exposed 100% surrounding medium—therefore pollution—direct flux equation translates contamination straight body burden. trophic contamination, however, essential know biomass specific item diet determine actual exposure (multiplying ingestion rates resource concentrations), finally calculate body burdens. steps can broken separate components, exactly careful attention required.

code: BTF_beetle <- 0.1    BTF_mammal_herb <- 0.05 BTF_mammal_ins <- 0.025 # 0.08 BTF_bird   <- 0.04  # (0.8 * 0.05) species_traits <- species_traits %>%   mutate(     BTF = case_when(       species == "beetle" ~ BTF_beetle,       species %in% c("myodes", "microtus") ~ BTF_mammal_herb,       species %in% c("apodemus", "sorex", "crocidura") ~ BTF_mammal_ins,       species %in% c("columba", "turdus", "athene") ~ BTF_bird     )   ) vec_BTF <- setNames(species_traits$BTF, species_traits$species)  # Définition des transferts de flux dans le spacemodel fluxes <- flux(     spcmdl_berisp_flux,      default = 1,     normalize = FALSE   ) |>   # 1. Contamination directe (les équations donnent le log10 de la concentration)   add_flux("soil", "plant",  ~ -0.488 + 0.494 * x) |>   add_flux("soil", "earthworm",  ~ 0.596 + 0.983 * x) |>   # 2. Invertébrés (beetle)   add_flux("soil", "beetle", ~ 10^x * vec_FIRbw["beetle"] * vec_BTF["beetle"]) |>   add_flux("plant", "beetle", ~ 10^x * vec_FIRbw["beetle"] * vec_BTF["beetle"]) |>   add_flux("earthworm", "beetle", ~ 10^x * vec_FIRbw["beetle"] * vec_BTF["beetle"]) |>   # 3. text: extract exposure (ingested dose) impregnation (body burden) without running model twice, can use simple mathematical trick. trophic network must propagate body burden prey predator, spatial model calculates final tissue concentrations default. However, since transfer equation animals strictly linear—Body Burden = Exposure × BTF—can easily retrieve initial exposure post-simulation using inverse operation: Exposure = Body Burden / BTF. implement cleanly R extract metrics final spatial model:

title: Berisp-like: a trophic model of contamination
text: spatial trophic modeling, crucial distinguish species’ habitat distribution (lives) foraging range (eats). foraging_kernels list provided transfer() function specifically defines foraging range: allows model scan surrounding pixels average contamination ingested prey. However, habitat maps already smoothed initial dispersal() step, must carefully select exposure_weighting method avoid mathematical error known double smoothing (applying kernel twice habitat): Avoid “diffuse”: apply spatial kernel second time habitat map, artificially expanding species’ presence. Use “potential”: maps pure environmental risk calculating theoretical exposure animal face placed given pixel, regardless actual habitat probability. Use “local”: calculates realized ecological risk weighting exposure strictly pre-dispersed habitat probability already calculated previous step.

Construction des seuils Eco-SSL (Calcul du Quotient de Danger - HQ) ecossl_threshold <- flux(spcmdl_berisp_flux, default = 1, normalize = FALSE) |>   # Végétaux   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "plant", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["plant"]) |>   # Invertébrés   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "earthworm", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["invert"]) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "beetle",    value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["invert"]) |>   # Mammifères - Herbivores / Omnivores   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "myodes",   value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["mamHerb"]) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "microtus", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["mamHerb"]) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "apodemus", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["mamHerb"]) |>   # Mammifères - Insectivores   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "sorex",     value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["mamInsect"]) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "crocidura", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["mamInsect"]) |>   # Oiseaux   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "columba", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["birdHerb"]) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "turdus",  value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["birdInsect"]) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "athene",  value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["birdCarn"])  # Apply the transfer to compute the spatial risk layers spcmdl_ecossl_risk <- transfer(   spcmdl_berisp_flux,   ecossl_kernels,   ecossl_threshold,   exposure_weighting="potential" )  # Risk colors breaks_risk <- c(-Inf, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, Inf) cols_risk <- c(   "darkgreen",   # 0 - 0.1   "green",       # 0.1 - 0.5   "lightgreen",  # 0.5 - 1   "yellow",      # 1 - 5   "saddlebrown", # 5 - 10   "#4A2C2A"      # > 10 )  names_keep <- names(spcmdl_ecossl_risk)[names(spcmdl_ecossl_risk) != "soil"] spcmdl_ecossl_risk_sub <- spcmdl_ecossl_risk[[names_keep]]  terra::plot(spcmdl_ecossl_risk_sub,             breaks = breaks_risk,             col = cols_risk)

title: A simple example: a soil-target transfer with fix or moving target
text: “Metaleurop” case involves 40 km² site northern France centered around former lead smelter. Soil levels around plant relatively high. extrapolated contamination maps Cadmium (Cd), Lead (Pb), Zinc (Zn) soil, derived 595 sampling points (extrapolation methodology covered vignette). cadmium map shipped package; lead zinc maps kept source repository (inst/extdata) read small helper, load_raster_repo().  Since 2006, total 1426 micro-mammals (representing 9 different species) captured -site measure bioaccumulation metals various organs (kidneys, livers). understand relationship soil contamination bioaccumulation, can categorize mammals two trophic groups: herbivores insectivores. plotting whole-body Cadmium concentration soil Cadmium concentration capture locations, can fit linear regression models establish basic transfer equations.
code: ground_cd <- load_raster_extdata("ground_concentration_cd_compressed.tif") ground_pb <- load_raster_repo("ground_concentration_pb_compressed.tif") ground_zn <- load_raster_repo("ground_concentration_zn_compressed.tif") ground <- terra::rast(list(cd=ground_cd, pb=ground_pb, zn=ground_zn))  terra::plot(ground) data("sf_micromammals") trophic_cat =  ifelse(sf_micromammals$genus %in% c("crocidura", "sorex"), "insectivore", "herbivore") sf_micromammals$trophic = factor(trophic_cat, levels = c("herbivore", "insectivore")) ptsHerb = sf_micromammals[sf_micromammals$trophic=="herbivore", ] ptsInsect = sf_micromammals[sf_micromammals$trophic=="insectivore", ]  lmH <- lm(log10(cd_WB_FW) ~ log10(cd_S), data = ptsHerb) lmI <- lm(log10(cd_WB_FW) ~ log10(cd_S), data = ptsInsect)  ggplot(data = sf_micromammals) +   theme_minimal() +   labs(title="Cadmium (Cd): log10(Whole body) ~ log10(Soil)",        x="Soil concentration (log10)",        y="Whole body concentration (log10)") +   scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +   scale_color_manual(     name="Trophic category",     values=c("#11aa44", "#aa4411")) +   geom_point(aes(x=cd_S, y=cd_WB_FW, color=trophic)) +   geom_abline(intercept=coef(lmH)[1], slope=coef(lmH)[2], color = "#11aa44", size=2) +   geom_abline(intercept=coef(lmI)[1], slope=coef(lmI)[2], color = "#aa4411", size=1.5) +   geom_abline(intercept= -1.2571, slope=0.4723, color = "red")

title: A simple example: a soil-target transfer with fix or moving target
text: Now validated transfer equations, can apply entire landscape map predicted Cadmium concentrations target species. First, extract median (50th percentile) parameter values fitted model use equations. Next, set spatial components: initialize spacemodel soil, herbivore, insectivore layers, establish direct trophic links, set dispersal kernels NA (since fixed-point model individuals move). Finally, define flux formulas using extracted parameters run transfer() function propagate contamination across every pixel grid. transfer() function outputs predictions log10 scale, inheriting scale input equations. visualize actual expected body concentrations, transform values back original scale (using 10^) map resulting layers using tidyterra ggplot2 logarithmic color gradient.  resulting maps display spatially explicit predicted body burdens target groups. expected direct fix-point model without dispersal, spatial patterns predicted concentrations directly mirror underlying soil contamination hotspots, scaled differently herbivores insectivores based distinct biological transfer rates.
code: dp_q50 <- df_pars %>%   dplyr::group_by(par) %>%   dplyr::summarise(median_value = median(value, na.rm=TRUE))  ls_q50 <- setNames(as.list(dp_q50$median_value), dp_q50$par) names_hab = c("soil", "herbivore", "insectivore") list_habitat <- lapply(names_hab, function(i) ground_cd) stack_habitat <- raster_stack(list_habitat, names_hab) trophic_df <- trophic() |>   add_link("soil", "herbivore") |>   add_link("soil", "insectivore") spcmdl_direct <- spacemodel(stack_habitat, trophic_df)  direct_kernels <- list(soil = NA, herbivore = NA, insectivore = NA)  direct_fluxes <- flux(spcmdl_direct, default = 1, normalize = FALSE) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "herbivore", value = ~ ls_q50$beta0 + ls_q50$beta1*x + ls_q50$beta_herbivore*x) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "insectivore", value = ~ ls_q50$beta0 + ls_q50$beta1*x + ls_q50$beta_insectivore*x)  spcmdl_direct_risk <- transfer(   spcmdl_direct,   direct_kernels,   direct_fluxes,   exposure_weighting="potential")

text: process involves two steps. First, TRV (Toxicity Reference Value) calculated. TRV represents safe daily ingested dose, expressed milligrams contaminant per kilogram animal’s body weight per day (mg/kg bw/day). one going use . , TRV used “back-calculate” maximum acceptable concentration soil (Eco-SSL) modeling animal’s diet. use equation: HQ=FIR×(Soil×Ps+Bi)TRV HQ = \frac{FIR \times (Soil \times P_s + B_i)}{TRV}

title: Implementing Eco-SSL model
text: solve equation HQ=FIR×(Soil×Ps+Bi)TRVHQ = \frac{FIR \times (Soil \times P_s + B_i)}{TRV}, table integrates several species-specific parameters: Surrogate Receptor Group: column identifies specific bird species chosen EPA represent entire dietary guild within ecosystem. instance, dove models avian herbivores, woodcock models avian insectivores (foraging soil), hawk models avian carnivores. TRV Cadmium (Toxicity Reference Value): maximum safe daily dose Cadmium bird can ingest without experiencing adverse health effects. avian species assessment, TRV set 1.47 mg/kg bw/day. Food Ingestion Rate (FIR): parameter represents total amount food bird consumes daily, normalized body weight (kg dry food per kg body weight). Notice insectivore (woodcock) highest metabolic demand ingestion rate (0.214) compared carnivore (0.0353). Soil Ingestion Proportion Diet (PsP_s): Birds incidentally swallow soil foraging preening. value represents fraction total daily diet made soil. ground-probing woodcock incidentally ingests soil (16.4% 0.164). Concentration Cadmium Biota Type (BiB_i): column provides bioaccumulation regression equations used estimate much Cadmium transfers soil bird’s specific food source (plants, earthworms, mammals). bridges gap environmental contamination dietary exposure. Eco-SSL (Ecological Soil Screening Level): final calculated threshold. represents maximum allowable Cadmium concentration soil (mg/kg dry weight) ensure target bird remains safe (HQ=1HQ = 1). avian insectivore risk, requiring stringent soil limit 0.77 mg/kg, carnivore protected 630 mg/kg.

B input soil concentration layers (x) currently log10log_{10}-scaled, must first back-transform actual, linear values (using 10^x) performing division. keep model setup clean easy update, first define vector containing specific Eco-SSL thresholds group, apply values within flux() function configure spacemodel object. easily interpret spatial distribution ecological risks, map calculated Hazard Quotients (HQs) using discrete, threshold-based color scale. HQ value 1 represents regulatory tipping point risk, palette split intentionally: areas threshold represented shades green (safe zones), areas exceeding threshold shift yellow dark brown (action risk zones). excluding baseline soil layer focus strictly ecological receptors, plot entire study area subsequently crop mask layers specific Metaleurop Region Interest (ROI) clean, site-focused evaluation.
code: # Define the Eco-SSL thresholds (in mg/kg) for each group in a named vector ecossl_vals <- c(   plant      = 32,   invert     = 140,   mamHerb    = 73,   mamInsect  = 0.36,   birdInsect = 0.77 )  # Build the Eco-SSL thresholds by transforming the log10 soil (10^x)  # and dividing by the specific Eco-SSL value to get the HQ ecossl_threshold <- flux(spcmdl_ecossl_h, default = 1, normalize = FALSE) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "plant", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["plant"]) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "invert", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["invert"]) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "mamHerb", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["mamHerb"]) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "mamInsect", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["mamInsect"]) |>   add_flux(from = "soil", to = "birdInsect", value = ~ 10^x / ecossl_vals["birdInsect"])  # Apply the transfer to compute the spatial risk layers spcmdl_ecossl_risk <- transfer(   spcmdl_ecossl_h,   ecossl_kernels,   ecossl_threshold,   exposure_weighting="potential" ) # Risk colors breaks_risk <- c(0, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, Inf) cols_risk <- c(   "darkgreen",   # 0 - 0.1   "green",       # 0.1 - 0.5   "lightgreen",  # 0.5 - 1   "yellow",      # 1 - 5   "saddlebrown", # 5 - 10   "#4A2C2A"      # > 10 )  names_keep <- names(spcmdl_ecossl_risk)[names(spcmdl_ecossl_risk) != "soil"] spcmdl_ecossl_risk_sub <- spcmdl_ecossl_risk[[names_keep]]  terra::plot(spcmdl_ecossl_risk_sub,             breaks = breaks_risk,             col = cols_risk) poly <- roi_metaleurop poly_vect <- terra::project(terra::vect(poly), terra::crs(spcmdl_ecossl_risk_sub))  rast_crop <- terra::crop(spcmdl_ecossl_risk_sub, poly_vect) rast_final <- terra::mask(rast_crop, poly_vect) terra::plot(rast_final,             breaks = breaks_risk,             col = cols_risk)

title: Spatial Environmental Risk Assessment Through Food Webs
text: example builds two habitat layers, links food web transfers cadmium soil consumer.
code: library(spacemodR)  # data shipped with the package: land cover and soil cadmium (log10 scale) data(ocsge_metaleurop) ground_cd <- load_raster_extdata("ground_concentration_cd_compressed.tif")  # 1. habitats: all the area for the soil, herbaceous cover for the consumer hab_soil <- habitat() |> add_habitat(ocsge_metaleurop) hab_vole <- habitat() |>   add_habitat(ocsge_metaleurop[ocsge_metaleurop$code_cs == "CS2.2.1", ])  stack <- raster_stack(   list(habitat_raster(ground_cd, hab_soil), habitat_raster(ground_cd, hab_vole)),   names = c("soil", "vole") )  # 2. food web: the consumer takes up the contaminant from the soil web <- trophic() |> add_link("soil", "vole")  # 3. spacemodel: the rasters and the food web together model <- spacemodel(stack, web) model[["soil"]][] <- ground_cd  # 4. transfer along the food web, with a Gaussian foraging kernel (sd = 200 m) kernels <- list(soil = NA, vole = compute_kernel(radius = 200, GSD = 25)) fluxes <- flux(model) |> add_flux(from = "soil", to = "vole", value = 0.5) exposure <- transfer(model, kernels, fluxes)  terra::plot(exposure)

title: Fit a variogram model to an empirical soil variogram — fit_soil_variogram
text: Fits one several theoretical variogram models empirical semi-variogram ([soil_variogram()]) weighted least squares, using weights \(N_j / h_j^2\) (number pairs squared distance), give importance short distances matter kriging (default `gstat::fit.variogram(fit.method = 7)`). Available models (`range` parameter meaning gstat): `"Exp"`: exponential, \(\gamma(h) = c_0 + c (1 - e^{-h/})\); `"Sph"`: spherical, reaches sill exactly \(h = \); `"Gau"`: Gaussian, smooth origin; `"Mat"`: Matérn smoothness `kappa` (`kappa = 0.5` `"Exp"`).

title: Rasterize a Habitat Object — habitat_raster
text: function maps continuous categorical weights habitat geometries onto raster grid. Background handling: default, pixels covered geometry assigned weight 0 considered passable (habitat = TRUE). Exclusion zones: Geometries added via add_nohabitat() act absolute barriers. pixel intersecting geometries assigned NA, overriding underlying weight. Stacking order: several features overlap, pixel takes value feature highest priority (see add_habitat); features stacked lowest highest priority top one read. equal priorities, order features habitat object decides (last top). add_habitat() add_nohabitat() give default increasing priority new layer, layers stack order added unless priority set explicitly. rule applies exclusion zones: non-habitat feature excludes pixel feature higher priority covers . Pixels filled feature: touches value feature (see add_habitat) sets pixels occupies. touches = TRUE (default add_habitat() add_nohabitat()) line polygon fills every pixel touches. thin structure hedgerow, river road chain pixels sharing edge: corridor stays connected 4-neighbour movements barrier crossed diagonally. touches = FALSE, polygon fills pixels whose centre covers line pixels thin line, keeps areas unbiased can break thin structures. Combine high priority touches = TRUE keep thin structure continuous layers runs . Points, lines polygons can mixed habitat object. Note raster holds one value per pixel: structure narrower pixel either widened full pixel dropped, two structures sharing pixel kept. matters, real solution finer ground_raster.

code: library(terra) #> terra 1.9.50 library(sf)  # Create a dummy reference raster ref_grid <- rast(nrows=10, ncols=10, xmin=0, xmax=10, ymin=0, ymax=10)  # Create habitat zones good_hab <- st_sf(geometry = st_sfc(st_polygon(list(cbind(c(1, 9, 9, 1, 1), c(1, 1, 9, 9, 1)))))) bad_hab  <- st_sf(geometry = st_sfc(st_polygon(list(cbind(c(4, 6, 6, 4, 4), c(4, 4, 6, 6, 4))))))  # Build habitat object my_habitat <- habitat() |>   add_habitat(good_hab, weight = 0.8) |>   add_nohabitat(bad_hab)  # Rasterize hab_rast <- habitat_raster(ref_grid, my_habitat) plot(hab_rast)   # A hedgerow kept continuous across the exclusion zone, whatever the order # in which the layers are added hedge <- st_sf(geometry = st_sfc(st_linestring(cbind(c(0, 10), c(0.2, 9.7))))) my_habitat <- habitat() |>   add_habitat(hedge, weight = 1, priority = 10) |>   add_habitat(good_hab, weight = 0.8, priority = 1, touches = FALSE) |>   add_nohabitat(bad_hab, priority = 2) plot(habitat_raster(ref_grid, my_habitat))

what: Gaussian kernel smoothing of soil concentrations — kernel_smooth_soil
title: Gaussian kernel smoothing of soil concentrations — kernel_smooth_soil
text: simple, assumption-light alternative kriging: value cell weighted mean sampled values, weights Gaussian function distance (Nadaraya-Watson estimator): $$\hat z(s) = \frac{\sum_i K(s - s_i) z_i}{\sum_i K(s - s_i)}$$ re-uses [compute_kernel()] (dispersal kernel package): points first rasterised (sum values number points per cell), rasters convolved kernel using [terra::focal()], ratio gives smoothed map. Unlike kriging, result honour data smoothing strength (`radius`) must chosen user, e.g. cross-validation [cv_soil()].

title: spacemodR 0.2.0
text: Refactored trophic fluxes interface: intake() function completely redesigned renamed flux() better reflect mathematical ecological concept transfer rates. New pipe-friendly syntax: definition transfer parameters longer uses multiple named arguments. Users must now initialize table flux() chain specific rules using new add_flux() function. Namespace conflict resolution: internal utility function previously named flux() (used within transfer() function) renamed avoid conflicts new main API.

title: spacemodR 0.2.0
text: New add_flux() function: Allows adding transfer rules readable, sequential manner (e.g., add_flux(= "soil", = "plant", value = ~ 10^x / 32)). Global target rules: add_flux(), source compartment () specified, rule (value) automatically applied links pointing target compartment (). Safe default values: flux() function now features explicit default parameter. highly recommended use 1 (full transfer) 0 (transfer) instead NA prevent propagation missing values subsequent model calculations.
